The Effects of Substrates on Arugula Growth
Background
In this experiment, arugula seeds were planted in a variety of soil-exolith mixtures with kelp. Our intent was to
test the effect of various fertilizers on the growth of plants once they germinated. Specifically, we were
interested in experimenting with the use of compost as a fertilizer, as the process of recycling food waste and
organic materials would help create sustainable practices in space food production. If successful, this could
provide astronauts a continual food source which would allow for an extended stay. However, based on initial
observations, our experiment was adjusted to determine the effect of using rinsed or unrinsed kelp on the
growth of arugula plants. Arugula was chosen based on the short germination period of approximately a week
(DIY Network, 2015) which would give a fast indicator of soil mixtures. Kelp was chosen as an additive to the
soil mixtures based on its micronutrients such as calcium, magnesium and boron (Bhatt, 2012). These are
required by the plant for chlorophyll production. Kelp can be dried and stored very compactly and still make a
great fertilizer that can easily be transported in space due to its small size and weight. When kelp is rehydrated
and mixed in with regolith, minerals and vitamins are released, enriching the soil with micronutrients
necessary for plant growth.
Experimental Design
Our experiment was designed to test fertilizer types and levels with a kelp and exolith mixture, however
through the experiment, it became apparent that our kelp and exolith mixtures would produce no plants. We
then adjusted to test if a kelp and exolith mixture that had the salt rinsed off of it (see Image 1) would produce
better results.
Our kelp and exolith mixture consisted of one cup of exolith and one half cup of dried kelp that was cut into
small pieces, approximately 5mm by 5mm. Each 5 inch round plastic pot was lined with 3 coffee filters to
encourage exolith and water retention throughout the experiment. The substrate mixture was then hydrated
for 24 hours prior to planting the arugula seeds in accordance with the package instructions (13mm deep).
Furthermore, once it was apparent that our (unrinsed) kelp and exolith conditions would not produce plants,
in addition to creating a rinsed kelp and exolith condition, we also decided to compare our soil only and exolith
only conditions to arugula grown in a sister study being conducted in our school. In this other study, types of
plants were being compared, but relevant for our study specifically were 4 pots of arugula. In this sister study,
arugula was being grown in either 1: one pot of soil only or 2: three pots of a soil and exolith mixture (one cup
exolith to half of a cup soil). By comparing these pots to our soil only, exolith only, and rinsed kelp and exolith
conditions, we were able to gather more information about growing arugula in a variety of conditions.
Hypothesis:
We hypothesized that if we cut up kelp into small pieces and added them into our exolith to create a mixture,
it would increase the surface area and thus increase the bioavailability of the nutrients to help support plant
2

growth within the exolith and also help the substrate retain water as the exolith is a very fine and sandy
substrate . When kelp is rehydrated it releases many required micronutrients needed for germination and
growth like calcium, magnesium, boron, etc. (Helmenstine 2019)
Independent Variables
Our independent variable is the type of substrate in each pot. We initially had one pot for a control of soil only,
one pot for a control of exolith only, and eight plants with a kelp and exolith mixture. We planned to use these
eight kelp and exolith pots to test fertilizer differences. However, once it became apparent that the kelp and
exolith mixtures did not allow any visible germination, we hypothesized that the salt on the kelp may have
been the reason for the lack of growth. We then created a new kelp and exolith pot, but with the kelp
thoroughly rinsed of all visible salt and replanted on March 17th, 3 weeks after the initial planting (see image
1).
Dependent Variables
We measured the average height of the arugula plants once per week for the 10 weeks of our experiment.
Measurements
The average height of the plants in each pot were measured once per week.
The Control Variables:
1.) Exposure to sunlight
The amount of light each pot received. All pots were located in the same southern facing bay window for the
duration of the experiment.
2.) Amount and frequency of watering
The amount of water the plants received is 50 mL every 3 days, measured using a graduated cylinder. All pots
were watered for the duration of the experiment, even the pots without sprouting plants.
3.) Pots that the plants were grown in
The plants were grown within eight plastic containers during the experiment. Each 4-inch container was lined
with 3 coffee filters. The coffee filters of the soil-only pot broke down near the top, and by week 6 the
above-soil filter paper detached and was recycled. It is believed that a portion of the filter paper still remains
below the soil. The pots contained manufactured holes to allow excess water drainage.
4.) Type of plant and seed depth
Each pot was planted with McKenzie’s Organic Arugula seeds. Four holes were created 13 mm deep to plant
the arugula seeds (see image 2) and then covered up with the soil type in each pot.
3

5.) Planting days
Seeds were planted on the same day (with the exception of the rinsed kelp and exolith pot) 13 mm deep (as
per seed package instructions.
Quantitative Results
Our soil only pot grew at a higher rate than both our exolith only and our rinsed kelp and exolith pots (Figure
1). The soil arugula grew to a total average height of 56mm in 9 weeks, while our exolith only arugula reached
a height of 39mm by the end of the experiment. The rinsed kelp and exolith grew to an above substrate height
of 9mm before dying.

Figure 1: Arugula Growth Through Time in Four Different Substrate Types
As evident in the graph, the seeds that were planted in the sister study (1, 2, 3, 4) grew better overall than the
seeds that were initially planted for this experiment (5, 6, 7). There were some considerable differences in
growing environments as the plants in the sister study were placed in a west facing window with a higher
average temperature than the seeds for this experiment which were placed in a south-west window with a
lower average temperature. This leads us to conclude that sunlight and temperature play a larger role in the
growth of arugula than initially expected and will be an important consideration in addition to soil composition
when recreating growing conditions on the moon.
Qualitative Results
Qualitatively, the exolith only plants did not appear as healthy as the soil only. They were not as tall, the leaves
have a smaller average surface area, were more yellow and less green than the soil only control condition (see
images 3 and 4).
Discussions and Conclusions
In conclusion, while our experiment did not produce the results we were expecting, we believe that we still
gathered important and useful information for the Plant the Moon research project. We stayed vigilant and
adjusted our course of action, by modifying our experimental design when the eight pots of kelp and exolith
failed to germinate any arugula. Rinsing our kelp before mixing it with the remaining exolith did produce a
more successful growth of arugula, even in the shortened time frame as the unrinsed kelp and exolith
5

condition. Further studies would focus on rinsed or freshwater kelp as an exolith additive for nutritional
purposes.
Furthermore, once it was apparent that the (unrinsed) kelp and exolith conditions did not produce plants, in
addition to creating a rinsed kelp and exolith condition, we decided to compare our soil only and exolith only
conditions to arugula plants grown in a sister study being conducted in our school. In this other study, types of
plants were being compared. Relevant for our study specifically, were 4 pots of arugula being grown in 1) soil
only (one pot) and 2) a soil and exolith mixture (3 pots of one cup exolith to half of a cup soil). By comparing
these pots to our soil only, exolith only, and rinsed kelp and exolith conditions, we were able to conclude that
heat and temperature may play a role in plant growth. One difference that we identified between the two
soil-only conditions (one in each study) was the temperature. The plants in the sister study were in a warmer
growing location than this study and therefore we need to factor in heat and temperature into future studies.
Another possible factor that led to the different growth rates could be watering amounts. In our sister study,
the watering schedule was kept more organic and plants were watered as needed (when the soil started to dry
out), yet still kept consistent across all pots in that study. In our study, watering was kept consistent at 50ml
every 3 days. It is a possibility that this led to overwatering some weeks and therefore may have impeded plant
growth in our study.
During our initial experimental design process, we were very interested in using compost to add fertilizer to
the exolith. However, this compost would require some time spent on the moon to produce food and organic
waste. Therefore, we decided to test kelp as a possible source of the initial nutrient needed upon landing on
the moon and adjust levels of fertilizer during the subsequent growing phase. We were not able to test this
due to the non-germinating state of these pots (see image 6).
During the post-experiment discussion, we discussed possibly breaking down the (rinsed) kelp into smaller
pieces, (perhaps with a blender) to further increase the bioavailability of the nutrients in the kelp. However, we
must pay attention to the fact that the exolith only condition produced taller and subjectively heartier plants
than our rinsed kelp condition (see images 3-5). Therefore, further studies should be conducted to determine
which inherent property of kelp hinders the growth of arugula. It is possible that some salt was not fully rinsed
out of the kelp, in which case, freshwater kelp may produce better results. It is also possible that another
property of kelp hinders plant growth. Perhaps a pH imbalance or some harmful chemical would be discovered
with further research and experimentation.
We also thought that the possible lack of microbial inoculants may have played a role in the poor plant growth
of the kelp and exolith conditions. We assume that the exolith provided did not contain a healthy ecosystem of
microbiotic life that Earth soil would contain. This may have also hindered the breakdown and release of
nutrients in the kelp additive.

The Effects of Plant Type on the Growth in Exolith and Soil Substrates
Background
In this experiment, arugula, carrots, beets, beans, and swiss chard seeds were planted in a soil mixture
composed of 1 cup exolith and ½ cup soil. Each plant type was chosen based on the high nutrition value (The
Old Farmer’s Almanac 2021) and which would require the fewest soil amendments (Plant The Moon Challenge
2021) it can offer to astronauts in space, and our ability to create the optimal growing conditions. In particular,
the leaves of carrots and beets are edible, making less waste and utilizing all components of the vegetable.
Since each plant requires different levels of macro and micro nutrients to grow, we designed this experiment to
observe the effect of the soil mixture on the growth of different types of seeds. A variety of different challenges
are presented when growing food in this mixture, including the low retention of water (Oliveira 2020) and the
high pH level of the regolith. Another factor is the small amount of reactive nitrogen and higher level of
aluminum present in regolith that can delay the growth of the plants or possibly lead to death. (Wamelink et al.
2014)
Experimental Design
Due to the Covid-19 pandemic and the amount of isolations occurring at the school level it was decided that
the plants would be grown in a house to maintain consistent growing conditions. The different arrays of plants
were kept in a west facing window that was warm in the afternoons. In this location plants received
approximately 6 hours of sunlight per day. Plants were watered frequently, on an as needed basis to ensure
they were not over watered, stripping the soil of the nutrients.
The development of this experiment was to determine favorable growing conditions for plants in exolith. To
determine the effects of the different soils, seeds were planted in a mix of exolith and soil (hereafter referred to
as exolith substrate) as well as only soil as an Earth control (hereafter referred to as earth substrate).
The types of plants chosen were arugula, swiss chard, carrots, green beans, and beets. Seedlings were
planted in one of the following potting configurations outlined in Table 1. The naming conventions of treatments
and the seeds were planted as per the directions on the package taking varying preferred depths into account.
Once sprouted, plants were rotated to strengthening the stems in relation to phototropism. As the plants grew
and the temperatures increased in the window, the plants were moved further from the window to prevent
wilting but maintain lighting conditions.

Hypothesis
If you plant a variety of seeds into pots containing both exolith and soil substrate they will grow at a different
rate (height) than plants growing in only soil, as exolith does not contain the microbes and is not as nutrient
rich as potting soil.
14

Independent Variables
The independent variable in our experiment is the seed type in the different substrates.
Dependant Variable
The dependent variable is the height the plant grew during the experiment.
Measurements
The height of the plants, the amount of water given to the plants, and the days the plants sprouted were
measured.
Control Variables
1.) Amount of sunlight
The plants were placed in a west facing window that received approximately 6 hours of direct sunlight a day.
The curtain on the window was open from approximately 7 am to 6 pm daily. The window got very hot in the
evenings and the plants were moved back from the windows. Plants were rotated both from front to back and
rotated by which side of the plant was facing the window to increase stem strength.
2.) Amount of water
The amount of water the plants received was 40 mL - 60 mL, depending on the growth of the plant. As the
plants got bigger the amount of water was increased, see raw data in the appendix.
Results
Green beans germinated in the earth substrate treatment, however, failed to germinate in the exolith substrate
treatments. All other plant species germinated in both the exoltih and earth substrate treatments. Germination
rates of arugula, bean, carrot, and swiss chard were greater in the earth substrate than in the exolith substrate.
However, the exolith substrate appeared to enhance the germination rate of beets.
Figure 1: Germination Rates Across Five Plant Species in Earth and Exolith Substrates
15

Successfully germinated arugula seedlings grew at a comparable rate in both exolith and earth substrates
(Figure 2). However, arugula seedlings grown in the earth substrate were generally approximately 3 cm taller
than the seedlings grown exolith substrate, indicating that this difference in height had developed before the
first height observation had been recorded. The arugula grown in the A3 appeared to grow at a slower rate
than the other arugula seedlings grown pots filled with exolith substrate (i.e., A1 and A2).
Successfully germinated beet, carrot, and swiss chard seedlings grown in an earth substrate grew at a faster
rate than those grown in the exolith substrate (Figures 3, 4, and 5). This resulted in the difference in height
between the two treatments to be greater between older plants than those observed in younger plants. Growth
rates of replicate exolith substrate treatments were highly comparable in the beet and swiss chard replicates.
The growth rates of carrots grown in exolith were generally comparable. However, growth in the third carrot
replicate pot (C3) stopped after day 30.
Raw data, code and photos located in the appendix.

16

Figure 4: Carrot Seeding Growth Over Time in Earth and Exolith Substrates

Figure 5: Swiss Chard Seeding Growth Over Time in Earth and Exolith Substrates
Discussions and Conclusions
As the experiment progressed it became clear that many of the plants grown in the exolith and earth substrate
did not grow as well as those in the earth substrate. The one exception to this was the arugula seeds in the
exolith and earth substrate, where the growth rate, although initially stunted, was similar to the growth rate in
the earth substrate. Therefore, we believe arugula would be an excellent candidate for the initial moon
gardens.
All plants grown in the exolith substrate had very thin stems. The bean plants did not sprout in the exolith
substrate, but they did in the earth substrate. As the stem for the bean is quite large, it is hypothesized that the
plant was not strong enough to break through the surface of the exolith/earth surface as the exolith created a
fairly solid top to the substrate. This idea is supported by observations made during watering where the water
would pool on the top of the substrate before draining through.
Another interesting finding that came out of this experiment was the variation of carrot growth in the exolith
substrate. It was found that the carrots grown in pot 3 stopped growing after day 30. This could be attributed
to the soil depth. Due to available pots, pot 3 for all plants was bigger but to keep the amount of exolith
substrate consistent the same amount of each was used in the bigger pot. This meant the pot 3’s had a
shallower depth of soil by 2cm. As carrots are a root vegetable it would be an interesting follow up experiment
to see if soil depth has an effect on the growth of carrots. It is also important to note that an effect of soil depth
was not seen in the beet seedlings during our 10-week study. Another interesting follow up experiment would
be to examine when in their growing phase do beets and carrots start growing their taproots, and would beets
be affected by soil depth (as the carrot plants were) given a longer growing condition.

Appendix 3: Analysis of data using code
germ <- read.csv("~/Documents/germination.csv", header=T)
png(filename="~/Documents/germanation.png", res=400, width=2500, height=2000)
par(mar=c(5,4,1,1))
barplot(as.matrix(germ), beside=T, xlab="Species", ylab="Germination Rate (%)", col=c(1,2),
names.arg=c(colnames(germ)[1:4],"Swiss Chard"))
legend(x=2, y=100,legend=c("Earth Substrate","Exolith Substrate"), col=c(1,2), pch=15, bty='n')
dev.off()
data <- read.csv("~/Documents/moonplants.csv", header=T)
names(data)
data$Day <- as.Date(data$Date)-as.Date(data$Planted)
data$Colour <- NA
data$Colour[data$Soil=="Earth"] <- 1
data$Colour[data$Soil=="Exolith"] <- 2
plants <- unique(data$Plant)
for(i in 1:length(plants))
{
temp <- data[data$Plant==plants[i],]
exo <- temp[temp$Soil=="Exolith",]
ear <- temp[temp$Soil=="Earth",]
exolm <- lm(exo$Height~exo$Day)
earlm <- lm(ear$Height~ear$Day)
filename <- paste("~/Documents/",plants[i],".png", sep='')
temp$potnumber <- substr(temp$Code, start=2, stop=2)
png(filename=filename, res=400, width=2000, height=2000)
par(mar=c(4,4,1,1))
title <- paste("Height (cm) as a Function of Days Since Planting of",plants[i],"Seedlings")
plot(temp$Height~temp$Day, col=temp$Colour, pch=NA, xlab="Day Since Planting", ylab="Height (cm)")
legend("topleft", legend=c("Earth","Exolith","*Digits indicate pot number"),pch=16, col=c(1,2,NA), bty='n')
uniquepots <- unique(temp$Code)
for(j in 1:length(uniquepots))
{
temppoints <- temp[temp$Code==uniquepots[j],]
points(x=temppoints$Day,y=temppoints$Height, pch=substr(temppoints$Code,start=2, stop=2), col=temppoints$Colour)
}
abline(earlm,col=1, lwd=3)
abline(exolm,col=2, lwd=3)
dev.off()
}
